name: Liarozole

lead: Liarozole is an investigational imidazole-type drug that raises the body's own retinoic acid levels by blocking its breakdown. The payoff in skin disease is smoother, less scaly skin through retinoid-style renewal.

It inhibits the CYP26 enzymes that degrade retinoic acid, and also inhibits aromatase and CYP17A1. It was studied orally in psoriasis, ichthyosis and prostate cancer; published trials concern skin disorders, not cosmetic skin aging. It is a forerunner of newer retinoic acid blockers such as talarozole.

paras: It was given orally in clinical studies of skin disorders. It is not available as an approved product, so there is no routine around it.
In a small psoriasis trial, itching, cheilitis and dry skin were most common. It is not approved for any use.

angle.text: Liarozole is an investigational drug that raises the skin's own retinoic acid by blocking its breakdown, aiming for smoother, less scaly skin. It was tested orally in psoriasis and ichthyosis; cosmetic use has not been studied.

lead: Liarozole is an investigational imidazole-type drug classed as a retinoic acid metabolism blocking agent (RAMBA). It inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzyme that breaks down all-trans-retinoic acid, raising retinoic acid levels in tissues, and it also inhibits aromatase and CYP17A1 [1][2]. It was studied orally for psoriasis, ichthyosis and prostate cancer [3][4][5].

It is not an approved cosmetic and its interest to appearance communities is indirect, as a forerunner of newer retinoic acid blockers such as talarozole. Published trials concern skin disorders, not cosmetic skin ageing.
infobox: Retinoic acid metabolism blocking agent (RAMBA); aromatase inhibitor [2]

paras: Retinoic acid is cleared by CYP26 enzymes. Liarozole blocks this clearance and in animal studies produced retinoid-like effects in vivo [6][1]. Reviews of RAMBAs discuss them as an approach to dermatological disease and cancer that raises endogenous retinoic acid rather than supplying a synthetic retinoid [1][7]. Laboratory work also showed liarozole inhibiting vitamin D 24-hydroxylase in prostate cancer cells [8].

In a randomized, double-blind pilot trial of 15 people with palmoplantar pustular psoriasis, oral liarozole 75 mg twice daily for 12 weeks produced significantly lower disease scores and fewer fresh pustules than placebo. The most common side effects were itching, cheilitis and dry skin; none led to withdrawal [3].

A randomized phase II/III trial in lamellar ichthyosis enrolled 98 people [4]. An earlier open trial in androgen-independent prostate cancer compared liarozole with prednisone [5]. No studies in cosmetic or photoaging use were found.

timeline.event: Liarozole shown to exert retinoid-mimetic effects in vivo [6].
